subject: pe

moments.title: Adams' closed-loop theory
moments.body: Adams' closed-loop theory of motor learning argues that movements are controlled by comparing ongoing feedback against a stored 'perceptual trace'. Practice strengthens the perceptual trace. The theory dominates motor learning textbooks for years before its limits become clear.
moments.takeaway: Closed-loop control explains slow movements but fails for fast ones — a ballistic golf swing cannot use feedback within the swing.

moments.title: Schmidt's schema theory
moments.body: Schmidt's schema theory replaces specific stored movements with general 'motor schemas' — rules that can produce variants. The theory explains why varied practice transfers better than blocked practice and why athletes can produce novel movements they've never specifically practised.
moments.takeaway: Athletes don't store every movement; they store rules for generating them. This insight shaped coaching for half a century.

now.title: Motor learning today
now.body: Constraint-led approaches (Newell, ecological dynamics) increasingly compete with schema theory in coaching practice. Variability in training, decision-training and skill-acquisition science (Mark Bennett's PDS Sports, Damian Farrow's work in Australia) shape elite training. Differential learning (Schöllhorn) embraces noise.
now.open_questions: Should coaching emphasise repetition or variability? Recent evidence favours variability for transfer but constraints in early learning.

reflection: Schmidt's schema theory was proposed by a graduate of Adams' lab. Theories in motor learning are taught as superseded; in practice they alternate and combine.
